> FreshFizz is a multinational soft-drinks business known for low-sugar flavours. It is thinking about entering **Country Z** by opening physical outlets and selling online. Local competitors are strong. A **sugar tax** on high-sugar drinks is being discussed by the government. Youth groups in Country Z often run online campaigns about healthy lifestyles.
> 
> **Table 4.1 – Market indicators for Country Z**
> 
> | **Indicator** | **Country Z** |
> |---|---|
> | Average monthly household  income | **£650** |
> | Population aged 15–24 | **27%** |
> | Internet users (share of population) | **84%** |
> | Import tariff on drinks | **10%** |

Should FreshFizz enter Country Z by franchising or through internal growth by opening company-owned outlets? Justify your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Local franchisees invest capital **[K]**, speeding up the rollout of the brand in competitive markets** [Ap]** and lowering FreshFizz’s risk. Fresh Fizz would need less cash for expansion, so it can focus on brand and supply chain **[An]**

However, if it opens company-owned outlets, FreshFizz would retail full control of pricing and customer service **[K]**. This would help protect its health-focused brand in a new country** [Ap]**, ensuring consistent customer experience and quicker response to changes to the sugar-tax** [An]**

FreshFizz should start with franchising to achieve quick growth with low capital requirements and low risk **[E]** in Country Z, using strong contracts and staff training to protect its brand. Once demand is proven, they may add some company-owned flagships in key cities for control and marketing impact **[E]**

> 
>   - State two valid points relevant to the question, each with a different viewpoint → 2 K marks

>   - Make a justified decision → 2 E marks
>

> 
>   - Franchising
>   
>     - Faster rollout using franchisees’ capital; lowers FreshFizz’s risk
>     - Local knowledge helps compete with strong domestic rivals
>     - Useful where 84% internet use supports centralised e-marketing and brand guidance
>   - Company-owned
>   
>     - Tighter control of pricing, service and health-focused brand in a sugar-tax context
>     - Easier to standardise product launches and respond to regulation
>   - Judgement
>   
>     - Speed needed to enter vs capital available
>     - Strength of contract/training to protect brand if franchising
>     - Market test approach: franchising for coverage + a few flagship company stores
>     - Youth market (**27% aged 15–24**) and online campaigns favouring consistent brand messaging

Titanic Toys (TT) could benefit from purchasing economies that would allow TT to get discounts when buying large quantities of materials to make toys **[Ap]**. This could lower costs and increase profits **[An]**. Technical economies would let TT use more specialised machines in its factory. TT already has some specialist equipment for flow production **[Ap]**, so it could add even more advanced machines to speed up toy manufacturing. This would increase efficiency and lower production costs **[An]**. Financial economies mean TT could borrow money more cheaply to fund its expansion plans **[An]**, like building a new factory in country Z **[Ap]**

Technical economies are likely to have the greatest effect on TT's profit  **[E]**. TT is already using flow production and lean methods like Kaizen **[Ap]**, so new specialised machines would fit well with its existing processes. More advanced equipment would speed up production significantly, allowing TT to make more toys in less time. This would lower the cost per toy **[Ap]** and increase productivity. TT could then either lower prices to be more competitive in country Z or keep prices the same for higher profits **[An]**

While purchasing economies could reduce material costs, TT may already get some bulk discounts **[E]** as a large company **[Ap]**. Financial economies would help with expansion costs, but TT might use its own money rather than borrowing **[E]**. Therefore, technical economies offer the biggest opportunity to lower production costs and increase output, leading to higher profits as TT grows and enters new markets like country Z **[E]**

**Furniture Outdoors (FO)**

FO has been a private limited company for 20 years. It is owned and run by the Chan family and is located in country Z. In country Z the secondary sector has become relatively more important as the country has developed. FO is a manufacturer of wooden furniture that is suitable for outdoor use. Its products include tables, chairs and other outdoor furniture.

Customers order online from the FO website. The furniture is then delivered to customers in country Z using FO’s own delivery vehicles. However, FO is considering changing to selling its furniture through either wholesalers or large retailers in country Z.

The Chan family have the business objective of contributing to sustainable development. FO only uses sustainably sourced wood when making furniture. This is from local forests in country Z and the wood is more expensive than imported alternatives.

For many years FO shareholders have reinvested profits to provide the finance for growth. FO recently took over 2 other furniture businesses in country Z and plans further takeovers. The Chan family plan to continue to control and manage FO after this expansion. The leadership style of these two companies is very different to that of FO and their factories are located several miles away from FO in different regions of country Z.

FO need to manage all its resources effectively. It tries to use the same components such as nails, brackets and paint for all its furniture designs. It is important to not run out of raw materials and so orders to suppliers must be carefully planned to avoid late deliveries. FO want to keep wastage of materials to a minimum. FO also need to consider how many employees are required to complete each order.

A report from the International Committee for the Planet states that manufacturers must find more sustainable ways to produce their products as global warming is becoming more of an issue.

The report suggests three main ways manufacturers can change:

parts.solution_md:
FO will likely find controlling the business the easiest problem to overcome. While FO now has three factories in different locations **[Ap]**, this challenge can be addressed by hiring more supervisors **[K] **to manage employees and improve communication across sites. Supervisors can relay messages between managers and workers at the three factories, ensuring employees are supervised properly and work efficiently **[An]**

The lack of finance could be harder to solve. As a private limited company, FO can only sell shares to family and friends **[K]**, limiting the capital they can raise. Taking out loans for expansion increases costs through interest payments, reducing profits. FO's 20-year history of success **[Ap]** may help secure loans, but this remains a significant hurdle **[An]**

The clash of business cultures may be the most difficult issue. The two companies FO took over had very different leadership styles **[Ap]**. Conflicts could emerge between staff resistant to change and management **[K]**, lowering efficiency and employee motivation. Overcoming ingrained workplace cultures takes time and careful management and may require training to minimise staff concerns **[An]**

While lack of finance and culture clashes are significant hurdles, they require complex,  long-term solutions **[E]**. Improving control through better management is a more straightforward fix that FO can implement relatively quickly **[E]**. With clear leadership and communication channels, possibly using technology to facilitate communication across its sites,  FO can maintain efficiency across its expanded operations **[E]**.

**Vegetable Palace (VP) **

VP was started 10 years ago in country Z. It is a public limited company. VP has a chain of 500 fast-food restaurants that operate across country Z. The VP brand is famous for its vegetarian food, this means none of its meals contain meat.

VP has a head office in Main City where all the directors and senior managers work. There are many barriers to communication. Each VP restaurant has a Manager, an Assistant Manager and 50 employees who cook and serve the meals. Restaurant Managers are often very busy and they are considering delegating some of their tasks to the Assistant Managers.

The ingredients for the restaurants are ordered in bulk by head office and then distributed from its warehouse to each of the restaurants. However, some senior managers think that Restaurant Managers should purchase their own ingredients from local suppliers. This would mean the ingredients would be fresher and would allow variations in the meals served.

VP wants to expand into another country. It will choose between the two countries shown in Appendix 2. VP will also need to decide how to enter a new market in another country. It has the option of forming a joint venture with another business or franchising the VP brand. The choice of finance will need to be considered for the expansion and the amount of finance will depend on the option chosen.

**Appendix 1 **

You will receive your meal in less than 5 minutes – guaranteed!

Delicious and varied meals for even the biggest of appetites and all at competitive prices.

**Email from VP’s Managing Director to VP’s Marketing Director **

Re: Economic changes in country Z

Did you see the news this morning that interest rates will be raised from 3% to 5% later today? This will have several effects on our business in country Z.

The news also said that the exchange rate in country Z has depreciated. We will have to consider how this will affect our business, especially as we import 30% of our ingredients into country Z.

There are also new legal controls being introduced that mean we have to list all the ingredients used in each of our meals on the menu. We do reprint menus every time we change the meals, but it is something to consider.

Consider the benefits and limitations of the following **two **ways VP can enter a new market in another country.

- Franchising

parts.solution_md:
A joint venture would partner VP with a local business, which could provide valuable knowledge about customer preferences, regulations, and suppliers **[An]**. For example, VP might learn which vegetarian ingredients are popular or how to adapt its menu to local tastes **[Ap]**. The partner could also contribute capital, reducing VP's financial risks **[An]**

However, joint ventures can lead to conflicts over control and decision-making. VP might disagree with its partner about menu changes **[Ap]** or quality standards, potentially damaging its brand reputation **[An]**

Franchising would allow VP to expand rapidly while maintaining control over its brand. Franchisees are responsible for start-up costs and local management, reducing VP's financial investment and risk **[An]**. This could be particularly beneficial if VP chooses Country A, where average meal prices are lower **[Ap]**, potentially limiting profitability

However, franchising might make it difficult for VP to ensure consistent quality across all locations **[An]**, such as its commitment to serve meals in under 5 minutes **[Ap]**

VP should choose franchising to enter the new market **[E]**. This option aligns better with VP's existing business model of operating a large chain of restaurants **[Ap]**. Franchising would use VP's strong brand and efficient operating procedures **[Ap] **while benefiting from franchisees' local knowledge and investment **[E]**. It would enable fast expansion, helping VP establish a strong presence before competitors enter the market **[E]**. It would also mean that, unlike in a joint venture, it would not have to share its success with another business **[E]**

>   - Apply it clearly to the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain how it works using a cause–effect chain → up to 2 An marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Relevant answers might include
> 
>   - Advantages
>   
>     - Can raise capital from the sale of shares – may raise more capital than a sole trader or partnership
>     - Limited liability – owners will not lose personal possessions if the business fails
>     - Separate legal identity – the company can be sued instead of the individual owners
>     - Continuity – the business continues even if shareholders change or die.
>     - Protection from unwanted takeovers – cannot be taken over without the consent of the shareholders
>   - Disadvantages
>   
>     - Cannot sell shares to the public – shares can only be sold to family and friends, which restricts the capital that can be raised
>     - Legal formalities when setting up – registration requires paperwork, time, and cost
>     - Financial statements must be publicly available – reduces privacy
>     - Shares are not easily transferable – transfer requires approval from other shareholders
>     - Accounts must be audited annually – increases ongoing administrative costs
